@iamadness69  Your first mistake is giving a fuck about what any of these talking heads are telling you. Go into forums, ignore the brand war bullshit and look at actual numbers/graphs. Compare that to what you WANT to use insert pc part here VERSUS what youll ACTUALLY end up using it for (step outside yourself, look back at your habits and see what youve done in the past with your computer. You can convince yourself that youre going to use it to get "so much work done!" and "im going to game SO HARD ON IT!", but if you look back and realize "oh, ive actually only ever used it to go on social media and played minecraft on it for 6 hours a week" then you know you dont need the top of the line, newest shit made this week).

comments.text: I would have really liked to see separate reviews for each of these cards.  Also just as a reminder not all of us get to play around with every gpu that comes out.  So for my instance I actually purchased a rx 7800 xt.  I was operating an rtx 2070 for the last 5 years.  I did not spend a dime on gpus during the pandemic overpricing.  I usually look for 50% more performance for the same price I paid for my previous card.  I steered clear of the last gen cards because of the pricing inflation.  Finally the 7800xt was the card that fit the bill.  I dont really care that the 6800xt is close in performance.  It was the bang for the buck I was looking for.  Also obviously Like most other people I rarely if ever use ray tracing.  It really  doesnt seem to bring too much to the table when it come to my enjoyment of a game.  Regardless the performance in the newer 7000 series amd gpu's is finally getting to a point when I may consider putting it on for a run through doom eternal since I am still getting well over 100 fps.  It seems only a couple of fames really suffer in ray tracing on Radeon.  Cyber punk and Alan wake 2.  Other games seem surprisingly comparative.  Say spider man remastered.  I am wondering since the tech is so new are these just not very well optimized for anything other then nvidia simular to applications that run cuda?  I guess time will tell.  I will most likely be rocking this rx 7800 xt in my rig for the next 5 years.  Thanks for letting me share my two cents.

comments.text:
As someone going all in on Team Red for GPUs (at least until I hear "Oh damn, Arc Battlemage/Chimera/Dragoon/whatever got hands now"), I sincerely do not care about frame generation or FSR 3. At least, I won't care about it for the next 5 years at least (you know, the correct use case for frame generation? prolonging the lifespan of your GPU? I remember the good old days). The only reason that seems to make sense to me about why everyone is up in arms about frame generation is that game developers (publishers and management, more likely) are dropping the ball with performance optimisation in all of the shiny, new, big AAAAAAA releases. 
Like, I'm not playing Starfield (it's a shame, as a medium length Elder Scrolls/Fallout fan, but I'm holding out until Bethesda either sells it for the price of a loaf of bread, or seems to learn from their mistakes), I have yet to play a lot of big releases from past years, let alone new ones, and my current shortlist of games I want to play are either oldish, low in performance requirements, or handled by devs who very much care about an optimised experience. I'm very much not affected by optimisation, at least outside of "This game is so old that running above 60fps makes everything run at increased speed", or "This game will not open on a system newer than Windows 7".

If I was more interested in playing something released in the last 3 months, I would just simply be more discerning about the games I play, and advocate for optimisations, rather than shackle myself to having half of the frames I see in games be technically incorrect at best and smeary, blurry, lossy artifacts at worst. It's not like there's a shortage of games that are super shiny or are beloved by gorillions of people, so just play something else.
Hopefully, the actual hardware side of GPUs gets a bit more promising sometime soon; if they start pushing each other on price, maybe AMD and Nvidia will start pushing on other fronts. Maybe. Perhaps. If we're good and eat our metaphorical vegetables. Or there will be no supper. We will only be allowed to sup on these metaphorical nuts.

comments.text:
Sorry, negative points are going first. Constructive criticism before admitting praise.

Cons:
1.1) In a review of primarily graming GPUs, why is there only ~3min of game data presented?
1.2) Why only show aggregated data? Were there no anomalous games where a subject GPU performed better or worse than expected against the competition? Were there no patterns in API or Game Engine performance, or even just the age of the games used? Were the subject GPUs most always aligned with the average trend, or is it a case of the average isn't reflective (i.e. you have 5 datapoints: +20% better performance, +15%, +10%, -20%, -25%. So geomean performance is ~98% ( =(1.2*1.15*1.1*0.8*0.75)^1/5 ), or about the same as the reference GPU. But in no single game is the subject GPU actually equivalent; either having more, a bit more, or much less performance.)
2) I do not like the selection of GPUs used for testing; 7800XT down to 5700XT, and 4070 down to RTX 2070.
An in one of the subject GPUs is expected to be the best performing GPU in the sample, alongside the 4070. This biases the visualisation (and the spoken words, if you're not listening carefully to the comments about the 6800XT) towards the 7800XT, making it look (and sound) like the best GPU available. Which can't be said because the higher performing GPUs are not shown to the viewer, which might be more expensive, but also more performent. Therefore the viewer may prefer to go for a better value, or know to avoid a worse value, higher-end option IF that data was presented.
3) Why talk about non-existing supporting software for longer than you show (not ever raw, but averaged) performance data on the screen?
Yes, mention FSR3 and AMD frame generation because it has tangential relevance to the subject under test. But when there is news and/or data to present, put that in a video on that subject!
4) Why include both 7700XT and 7800XT in the same review? 20min is a long video for LTT. But as I am hopefully pointing out, the video did not present much data and spent most of the time talking about conclusions.

Pros: 
1) The graphs that were included looked clean and were easy to decypher. Pat on the back for whoever does data visualisation.
2) The video felt more mature, more like a data-driven review than an opinionated news article - which is how I used to interpret LTT reviews, even before the whole fiasco, which isn't to say I ignored them in the search for a well-rounded perspective.
3) Kudos for putting the term "geomean" front and centre, although it was never explained why that was done. Bearing in mind, the argument behind the previous LTT review style was a less technically-minded audience... Does the viewer know what geomean is? Or arithmetic mean (a.k.a. just the mean )?

comments.text: 15:10 Quick note on this: DLSS/DLAA are the same thing just that dlaa skips the upscaling step which makes it the same as AMDs alternative setup. You are right in pointing out that this makes it very similar to TAA, except that is also the case for NVIDIAS alternative. DLSS is, in fact, an implementation of TAA using machine learning. I have integrated DLSS in an engine and it simply replaces that pass in rendering taking the same inputs and outputs as normal TAA would. This isn't to talk down this tech, but the innovation is in how well these technologies do TAA, not in what they do. Conventional TAA can also be implemented in a way that does upscaling and frame generation, just not nearly as well as DLSS does.

comments.text:
The patent from mega pro, the cost of the dye, coloured plastic. All add up.
The dye alone is tens of thousands, the patent likewise is not cheap and coloured plastic for injection moulding can get way more expensive than you'd expect.
The reality is, the screwdriver is legitimately a high quality tool and has a price to go with it. That's both covering the cost of the machine for injection moulding, product shipment and per unit cost are all pretty expensive. I'd wager the screwdrivers would cost ~$20-$30 to make. Then they need to add on the cost of storage, and shipping and minimum order quantities. Not to mention how theyd have to change the plastics and dyes every time they release a new colour. Mass production makes stuff cheaper, but it's by no means cheap. If you look at other ratcheting screwdrivers in the same ballpark of quality they have undesirable parts to them or are way more expensive.

Built a computer last week, went Intel for the chip (which came with Nightingale and Assasin's Creed: Mirage, for values of "came with" that include "will eventually allow me to play when those games release if I remember to redeem them on time") and AMD's RX 6800 for the video card, which came with Starfield which I would have bought anyway.

So far at 1440, I think the only game I'm not a full ultra, no upscaling, is Starfield. I think Baldur's Gate 3 was ultra, but I'm not sure I checked, it looked great though. 

But everything else I play? It does just fine. I'm graduating from a laptop with a 15 inch HD screen, a 6th gen I7 and a GTX 950m 4g graphics card, with 16 gigs of system ram, to a desktop with a 13th gen I5, RX 6800 and 64 gigs of DDR4 because my rule of thumb for the last twenty years was to spend about a hundred on RAM and why the heck not. Oh, and a 27 inch 2k monitor. The leap in size, crispness and speed is so much that anything else would have been overkill. I wasn't going to spend $500+ on a new video card. This one was $429 and was the single most expensive thing in the case. 

Other games I've tried so far include Skryim (laughably fast, there aren't loading screens, it's wild), Subnautica, BZ, No Man's Sky (which is probably the most demanding of my "old" games), Fallout 4... and my god, it is so nice to play them at higher frame rates. IDK what I was getting on the laptop but I capped my frame rate on the whole system to 120 fps for reasons, the monitor can go up to 165 but it's a cheap monitor and was having some odd behavior at the highest frame rates and causing blinding headaches. But even that's double the maximum possible I was getting before.

These results do not match Puget System's results, which imo are more reliable.
During a very long time, nvidia cards have done better for Davinci.  They only tried two things here, and not sure in which conditions. Check for the most recent articles and reviews with benchmarks and text from Puget Systems, they do a quite wider testing (and imo more serious). They work for video-professional customers. A 3080 IMO is a VERY good card for Davinci. Don't worry about it. A 4070 is way better, but the amount of VRAM and the kind of projects you do is a very important factor (specially if working a lot at 6k or higher, and/or very complex projects in terms of effects and etc).

But their conclusions do match with puget with what they mention about the 4060 ti.  That card, despite being really good in power consumption, does perform WORSE than the 3060 ti, which is crazy. Due to the cuts made in this generation. 

A 4070 12GB (no need for the 4070 ti, is incredibly close in performance in Davinci) for 2D/3D productivity is IMO a sweet spot in terms of performance/cost, unless you can go for a 4080 16GB. As the 4070 also does perform GREAT in Blender (and I guess in many 3D softwares).

comments.text: can you explain why geometric mean is better than regular mean or median for a lognormal distribution?
comments.author: @MatthisDayer

comments.text: @MatthisDayer  With Geometric means, the average is less affected by spikes in the numbers compared to the average. So in this case, if the graphics cards had a part of the game/test where they momentarily saw 200 FPS (for example), but on average only had 50 FPS, the geomeans will produce a value that is closer to where most of the recorded FPS sits. Whereas the means (average) will likely be higher because it is more influenced by those spikes in the data. By showing the geomeans, we can get a better sense of what someone will experience using the cards. This of course requires that your data is lognormally distributed but there are tests for that. The median is a close approximation of the geomeans because it is the value where 50% of the data points are below it, and 50% of the data points are above it. The median will approximate the geomeans when there is consistency in those data but since is not an average, if there are patches of repeated values the geomean will better incorporate those to give a more informative value.

comments.text:
The 7800 XT is a successor to the 7700 XT, and it is a big improvement over the 6700 XT's launch MSRP, especially if you properly account for inflation, which has been a lot higher than normal over the last three years. 

The 6700 XT launched at 480 USD, which is equivalent to about 540 USD today. That was a bloated MSRP because of the GPU shortage, so it was probably originally planned to be a lot closer to 425. Even still, 425 in early 2021 is equivalent to around 485 USD today, and the 7800 XT is around 43% faster than the 6700 XT, with 33% more Vram, more memory bandwidth, and various other features and improvements, so that's still a significant improvement in value even over whatever the 6700 XT would have launched at if there hadn't been a GPU shortage at the time. 

The 5700 XT, which was launched in 2019, and was considered a very good value at the time for 400 USD, would be equivalent to about 480 USD in 2023 as well, and the 7800 XT is somewhere around 90% faster, with double the Vram capacity. 

We are definitely still seeing significant gen on gen improvements, it's just that we've already been seeing a lot of heavily discounted previous gen AMD cards, so the 7800 XT isn't super exciting compared to those, but only if those cards were actually available at those discounted prices in your region, and unfortunately, those heavy discounts on RX 6000 series cards just haven't been very widely available outside of the US (even in Canada, it was a lot harder to find really good prices on RX 6000 series cards for some reason).

comments.text:
So you noticed that the arithmetic mean is not an appropriate central tendency for FPS, a frequency,  and you switched to the geometric mean. In a sense, it is a better measurement of the central tendency, but only because the geometric mean is always closer than the arithmetic mean to the harmonic mean, which you should have used. 
A way of finding the appropriate central tendency is to ask yourselves: What is a natural operation between two measurements of FPS? 
Some examples:
1. Two people have apples. One has 5. The other has 9. Addition is a natural opperation over countables, so the arithmetic mean is appropriate. The mean is (5+9) / 2 = 7.
2. My investment portfolio in day one obtained a 10% profit and in the second day a 15% loss. A natural operation between returns is multiplication, so the appropriate mean is the geometric mean. Its value is ((1+0.1) * (1 - 0.15 )) ^ (1 / 2) ~= 0.97 => a 3% loss overall.
3. The natural opperation between measurements of time is addition (I can wait 3 minutes and then I can wait 5 more. The result will be that I waited 3+5=8 minutes). The inverse of FPS is a measurement of time. We can compute the arithmetic mean of these measurements of time. To convert the resulting average frame time into FPS we would need to invert it again, thus obtaining the harmonic mean of the FPS values over multiple games.

comments.text:
As a BI consultant, I'd just wanted to congratulate to you for working on your visualizations. But I honestly think you've stepped in the wrong direction. 
Bar/Column charts:
- Gradient is bad. It confuses, it's heavy on the eyes. Never use it
- Font size in the data label should be in a way that it doesn't get through boundaries of visualization 
- If you are comparing two sets of GPUs, it'd be good to give them same color (Red and green, it's pretty obvious). The rest (not part of this benchmarks) could be gray. This would help with orientation without the annoying highlight
- On the opposite note, I want to thank you for the 30/60/120 gridline. That was actually sensible addition
The line charts: 
- I can get behind this for the purpose of showing how messy it actually is (FPS over time)
- Just maybe darker color for tthe X/Y axis and bigger transparency for the gridlines as in this case the gridlines are little bit misleading
- In the end it will be always messy, but you can highlight first/last or min/max or average run(which is actually not here) 
- I believe you can show power consumption as % change in time, especially if you want to compare multiple series. Tell me what is the exact diffference between 7700XT and 7800 XT? You can't tell from the graph, because they are overlapping. Is the goal to show actual consumption or the change? This tries to do both and terribly. Two separate graphs with less detailed granularity for consumption over time and then second chart with detailed % change over time will be better for understanding the point made here. Dotted lines really doesn't make a sense in this level of granularity, you cannot see it. It would make a sense comparing 6th vs 7th generation e.g. or x800 vs x700
Tables:
- Honestly I am not fan of pictures in tables, especially blurred behind table. I'd put it on the top of the table horizontally and call it a day and focus on simpler no effects table. 
Generally:
- Colour scheme is (kind of) okay, but I think you don't have your LTT theme created/implemented. Each visualization is on each own and it doesn't fit "LTT" or the products. As much as you criticize AMD for naming convention, same should be done for colours. 
- I like you are sometimes highlighting what you are talking about. Good job, I think it's not overdone
- Dark schemes are hard to do correctly for visualizations. The contrast, strain on eyes. I am generally not fan of it 


As an ending note: If everything scream it's important, nothing is important


This is maybe nitpicking in your eyes, but I want to be critical in constructive way. I see each day a lot of design mistakes but in the end, visuals are always kind of subjective. But I believe my critics is trying to be objective. So take it with a grain of salt just as a point for discussion

comments.text:
Remember people, DLSS3 is also just upscaling, the framegen is 'just a part of it' (This is needed to understand DLSS 3.5 😉). And the framegen in FSR3 has the same thing has the framegen in DLSS3 -> It's only worth it if the game is already running good and stable over 40fps. And probably requires a VRR screen, or you will have to play it vsync'd. Which at 60fps is quite a bad idea (remember that the input latency is than less than a normal 30fps game). Vsyncing at 120fps is fine and gives a fine latency like a native 60fps game. Which is more than good enough for most players :).
'AMD fluid frames' is a driver level implementation that works on almost any game, but that WILL mean: Only works on 7000 cards (and maybe 6000 cards, but that's it I believe), and you will; get more artefacts, because it has issues with things like the HUD and other elements on screen, just like your TV would have. Please don't get your expectations up that every game that had issues to hit a good 30fps you can now easily play at 50fps or something... it doesn't work like that.

comments.text: It really feels like AMD is trying to catch up. But honestly from gamer and developer input.... it feels like no one cares. I mean... they will care of just having something else to temper prices. It really does feel like AMD may end up leaving the consumer GPU space. They make plenty from their APUs and mobile chips. They are also pulling market share in the server space. But it feels like they are not making any progress to pull consumers away. So often in the comments section I'll see people being "excited for AMD; happy for competition; maybe I'll switch to AMD for my next build." But according to the independent sales reports... that's not happening. Consumers are choosing to actively not vote with their earnings. People got mad at AMD for default implementing FSR support instead of DLSS in Starfield. To recap... people got mad for AMD supporting the open platform almost any graphics card can use, instead of DLSS from day one. I would understand this if it were new, but this isn't. Nvidia has been paying game and software developers for years to push better integration of their implementations and frameworks for over a decade. To the point that many productivity applications are heavily skewed in Nvdia's favor and barely support other GPU options. AMD is trying to push and support open source projects, but that doesn't seem to be taking off. Right now with how jaded gamers are... I don't see a future where AMD could overtake Nvidia.

comments.text:
The 7800 XT is a successor to the 7700 XT, and it is a big improvement over the 6700 XT's launch MSRP, especially if you properly account for inflation, which has been a lot higher than normal over the last three years.

The 6700 XT launched at 480 USD, which is equivalent to about 540 USD today. That was a bloated MSRP because of the GPU shortage, so it was probably originally planned to be a lot closer to 425. Even still, 425 in early 2021 is equivalent to around 485 USD today, and the 7800 XT is around 43% faster than the 6700 XT, with 33% more Vram, more memory bandwidth, and various other features and improvements, so that's still a significant improvement in value even over whatever the 6700 XT would have launched at if there hadn't been a GPU shortage at the time. The 7800 XT is also a big improvement in value per dollar over the 6800 XT's launch price in 2020.  

The 5700 XT, which was launched in 2019, and was considered a very good value at the time for 400 USD, would be equivalent to about 480 USD in 2023 as well, and the 7800 XT is somewhere around 90% faster, with double the Vram capacity. 

We are definitely still seeing significant gen on gen improvements, it's just that we've already been seeing a lot of heavily discounted previous gen AMD cards, so the 7800 XT isn't super exciting compared to those, but only if those cards were actually available at those discounted prices in your region, and unfortunately, those heavy discounts on RX 6000 series cards just haven't been very widely available outside of the US (even in Canada, it was a lot harder to find really good prices on RX 6000 series cards for some reason).

comments.text:
Please, just stop using Cyberpunk as an indication of RT performance. The RT code in that game was written years ago by NVIDIA for RTX cards at a time when RDNA2 didn't even exist. 

CP'77 is an NVIDIA showcase for NVIDIA cards on a now dead engine which will never power another game. This game will heavily skew your RT results and you're not exactly balancing that out with a single other RT game.

This is not what you should be looking at if you care about showing expected RT performance going forward. You are giving people the wrong idea when focusing on this legacy title. 

People might want to know that the 7800XT basically matches the 4070 in :

Metro Exodus EE
Spider-Man: Remaster / Miles Morales
Resident Evil 4 / Village
Fortnite 
Star Wars Jedi Survivor
DOOM Eternal
Watch Dogs: Legion

And over a larger sample of RT games, including outliers like CP77, we see the difference is only around 15% overall with a win to the 4070 (which costs $100 more).

The most important game in that list might be Fortnite since that uses UE5, and engine which will power many next-generation games and is a much more valuable indication of RT performance than Cyberpunk.

comments.text:
1 question and 1. Comment and 1. Bonus comment for good faith constructive feedback (unlike what Steve did.).
1. Why are you using the geometric mean instead of arithmetic mean? As a general rule, measures of means of a set of independent events with same units (like repeated benchmarking of GPUs).
2. If presenting mean values, you need to provide sample size, error bars (or at least the margin of error/95% confidence interval, and range of sample values. 150fps ±100fps is wildly different from 150fps ±5fps. 
3. Bonus comment: if comparing between models, you should really be running the benchmarks at least 30 times per card and run a 2-sample t-test to determine if the mean values between models are significantly different. (There are other methods for testing smaller sample sizes, but they’re less accurate).

Fortunately, all of this can be easily automated.
comments.author: @samlevi4744

comments.text: Why would they use an arithmetic mean to compare across games? Arithmetic mean would only make sense if averaging across the same game.
comments.author: @sw2598

comments.text: @sw2598  care to explain your logic behind that claim? I mean, without seeing the raw data to calculate variance and skew and check for outliers I cannot definitively rule out high variability, positive skew, or large outliers. But Geomeans are primarily used for percentage data, highly variable data, positively skewed data, or data that is dependent on other values in the set, or data using different units. Comparing across a non-random sample of games has some issues in its own, but it also has a greater chance of having an abnormal variance (high or low) and excessive positive skew or massive outliers. That said, unless those are present, there would be no reason use geomeans over the more accurate arithmetic mean (more accurate for the type of data and unit of measure present). Geomeans obviously have their place, but this isn’t it unless certain conditions are met. Given that those conditions are not the expected norm, descriptive statistics that justify using Geomeans should have been provided..

comments.text:
That's an issue caused by marketing, not products themselves. AMD decided to add a new highest tier to bring back XTX naming, and it consequently pushed everything up a tier.
7900XT -> 7900XTX
7800XT -> 7900XT
7800 -> 7900GRE
7700XT -> 7800XT
7700 -> 7700XT
Generational increase in performance is there, but unfortunately it's in line with the price increase.
I suppose messing up the naming was the way to increase actual gen-over-gen MSRP.
Reviewers tend to focus a lot on MSRP as it's a nice number marketed everywhere, but it's the real world retail pricing that truly matters. It is highly variable based on region and availability, so it's pretty much impossible to evaluate for reviewers. For example, I got my 7900XT in March far cheaper than my friends got their 6800XT/6900XT/3080 a year prior during the shortage. Every reviewer under the sun was saying how much better value the 7900XTX is, but for me 7900XT was 900€, XTX was 1200€.
